evidence.note: Writer resolves the store via git rev-parse --path-format=absolute --git-common-dir through deps.Exec (gate.RealExec, GIT_* scrubbed)
Reader StoreDir uses the same scrubbed gate.RealExec and the same rev-parse flags; StoreDirIn is the one layout definition, also used by session bindings
RealDeps wires Exec to gate.RealExec, and Store/Sidecar/Terminal all take the common dir, so runs, sidecars and ledger agree on <common>/metareview
record-lenses --from-run reads <common>/metareview/runs first and falls back to the 0.13.x main-checkout location with a warning, matching where the FSM writes and what it migrates
Migration ordering: roots() migrates runs, then ledger rows, before any Store/Exists/peek call in init, openRun and diff; status paths are read-only and report pending legacy runs instead
Abandoned-run discovery scans the legacy location then the store (dedup by id), so a rename mid-scan is never missed; per-worktree attribution by init work_dir
FSMRunDir is now relative to the common dir in both RowFor and MigrateLegacyRows, matching docs/ARCHITECTURE.md
Docs describe the common-dir store, the ledger, the migration lock and legacy fallback consistently with the code
Targeted go test over internal/fsm/run, record, status, repo, session, machine, and -run Migrat|Root|Store over internal/fsm/cli and cmd/metareview: all ok at 58e2308

findings.note: Stale comment: appendRow still says runs.jsonl has a second, lock-free writer (state.AppendJSONL). Since #173 the FSM ledger is <common>/metareview/runs.jsonl, which only record writes; the review gates keep appending to the checkout's .metareview/runs.jsonl. O_APPEND is harmless, but the rationale is now wrong.

MigrateLegacyRuns moves each run with os.Rename. If git's common dir is on a different filesystem from the main checkout (for example --separate-git-dir on another volume), rename returns EXDEV and roots() fails every fsm command until the user moves the runs by hand. This setup is uncommon. A copy fallback, or an error that tells the user what to do, would make it recoverable.
